- If sentiment is positive (≥ 0.0) in the last 3–5 days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–2% for next 5–7 days.  
- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.3) and prices are rising, model often overshoots; cap forecast at 1–2% above recent peak.  
- If model shows strong upward momentum (e.g., 3+ consecutive rising forecasts) and sentiment is neutral or slightly negative, reduce forecast slope by 10–15% to avoid overcorrection.  
- If true outcome shows sharp spike (e.g., >5% from prior day) and model fails to catch it, adjust forecast to match sentiment direction — if sentiment is bullish, model should not lag more than 1–2 days.  
- If model consistently underestimates true price in the last 5–7 days (especially after sentiment turns positive), add 0.5–1.5% to forecast for next 3–5 days.  
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating +/–) and model is averaging, use sentiment-weighted smoothing: assign 70% weight to recent sentiment, 30% to historical trend.  
- If model forecast is >10% above true outcome for 3+ consecutive days, assume overconfidence; reduce forecast by 2–3% per day until sentiment stabilizes.  
- If sentiment is negative and model forecast is rising, check for lag: if true price is rising faster than model, adjust forecast to match sentiment direction — don’t wait for 2+ days to react.  
- If sentiment is positive and model is flat or falling, model may be underestimating bullish momentum — increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day for next 3–5 days.
